title: Managing Workflow Failures
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of managing workflow failures and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to managing workflow failures.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on managing workflow failures. Retries should be limited to plausible transient failures; keep failed-run evidence, preserve clear failure status, and document escalation/incident steps. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Managing Workflow Failures matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Retries should be limited to plausible transient failures; keep failed-run evidence, preserve clear failure status, and document escalation/incident steps. Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Retries should be limited to plausible transient failures; keep failed-run evidence, preserve clear failure status, and document escalation/incident steps. Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Identifying flaky tests
items.text: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. Preserve reports where useful and configure required branch checks to match the checks the workflow actually emits.

items.title: Retrying transient failures
items.text: Start with the first failed step and its exit code, then inspect the event, conditions, permissions, tool versions, network, and runner state. Capture sanitized diagnostics and preserve evidence of the failure.

items.title: Distinguishing application failures from platform failures

items.title: Avoiding blind retries
items.text: For avoiding blind retries, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Preserving failed-run evidence
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Escalation and incident documentation
items.text: For escalation and incident documentation, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

content_blocks.code:
steps:
  - name: Record a sanitized diagnostic
    if: ${{ failure() }}
    run: echo "A prior step failed; inspect its exit code and sanitized logs" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
content_blocks.expected_output: When a prior step fails, the summary adds a reminder to inspect logs without reproducing environment values or secrets.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a test repository or static validation first. Confirm the snippet matches the repository, runner, permissions, and current GitHub documentation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove temporary test workflows and never carry test credentials or sample outputs into production.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to managing workflow failures. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain managing workflow failures, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Turn run status, logs, and diagnostic data into a systematic troubleshooting process.

content.task: Apply managing workflow failures to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Retries should be limited to plausible transient failures; keep failed-run evidence, preserve clear failure status, and document escalation/incident steps.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Retries should be limited to plausible transient failures; keep failed-run evidence, preserve clear failure status, and document escalation/incident steps. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Retries should be limited to plausible transient failures; keep failed-run evidence, preserve clear failure status, and document escalation/incident steps.

Debug the earliest failing step first. Use the event payload, job/step logs, exit codes, runner state, permissions, and sanitized diagnostics to separate configuration failures from infrastructure failures.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
